# Summary

Visium HD measures gene expression in 2 µm squares, which are usually
analysed after binning them into 8 µm or 16 µm bins. Compared to the
datasets in the other tutorials, such a dataset has

- **very many pixels**: hundreds of thousands of 8 µm bins instead of a few
  thousand spots, and
- **few counts per pixel**: a few hundred instead of tens of thousands.

`STdeconvolve` works on such data, but two default settings were chosen for
datasets with a few thousand large spots and should be changed:

1. `removeBelow` of `restrictCorpus()` removes the genes that are detected in
   few pixels. Its default of 5% removes the marker genes of every cell-type
   that covers a small part of the tissue.
2. `max.counts` of `fitLDA()` fits the models on a random subset of the
   pixels. This is many times faster and gives the same models, because the
   gene expression profiles of the cell-types are well determined by far
   fewer than all pixels.

This tutorial shows both on the 8 µm bins of a mouse kidney, and ends with
what to expect from the 2 µm squares.

# Data

We use the [Visium HD mouse kidney
dataset](https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets/visium-hd-cytassist-gene-expression-libraries-of-mouse-kidney)
of 10X Genomics. The counts of all bin sizes are in one archive (9.5 GB), of
which we need the filtered count matrix and the bin positions of the 8 µm
bins, and the count matrix of the 2 µm squares for the last section.

```{r download}
f <- "visiumHDTutorial/"
files <- c("binned_outputs/square_008um/filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5",
           "binned_outputs/square_008um/spatial/tissue_positions.parquet",
           "binned_outputs/square_002um/filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5")

if (!all(file.exists(paste0(f, files)))) {
  dir.create(f, showWarnings = FALSE)
  options(timeout = 3600)
  archive <- paste0(f, "Visium_HD_Mouse_Kidney_binned_outputs.tar.gz")
  download.file(paste0("https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/spatial-exp/3.0.0/",
                       "Visium_HD_Mouse_Kidney/Visium_HD_Mouse_Kidney_binned_outputs.tar.gz"),
                destfile = archive)
  untar(archive, files = files, exdir = f)
}
```

The count matrices are stored in the HDF5 format of 10X Genomics. This
function reads one as a sparse genes x bins matrix. It needs the `hdf5r`
package; the bin positions are read with the `arrow` package.

```{r read_function}
library(STdeconvolve)
library(Matrix)
library(ggplot2)

read10xH5 <- function(file) {
  h5 <- hdf5r::H5File$new(file, mode = "r")
  on.exit(h5$close_all())
  m <- h5[["matrix"]]
  sparseMatrix(i = m[["indices"]][] + 1L,
               p = m[["indptr"]][],
               x = as.numeric(m[["data"]][]),
               dims = m[["shape"]][],
               dimnames = list(make.unique(m[["features/name"]][]),
                               m[["barcodes"]][]))
}
```

```{r load}
cd <- read10xH5(paste0(f, files[1]))
dim(cd)

pos <- as.data.frame(arrow::read_parquet(paste0(f, files[2])))
## position of each bin on the grid of bins. Rows are counted from the top.
pos <- data.frame(x = pos$array_col, y = -pos$array_row, row.names = pos$barcode)
pos <- pos[colnames(cd), ]
```

There are `r format(ncol(cd), big.mark = ",")` bins. Half of them have fewer
than `r median(colSums(cd))` counts:

```{r libsize}
summary(colSums(cd))
```

# Cleaning

We keep the bins with at least 100 counts.

```{r clean}
counts <- cleanCounts(cd, min.lib.size = 100)
dim(counts)
```

# Selecting genes: `removeBelow`

`restrictCorpus()` selects the genes for the model in two steps. It first
removes the genes that are detected in more than a fraction `removeAbove` or
in less than a fraction `removeBelow` of the pixels, and then keeps the (up
to `nTopOD = 1000`) most overdispersed of the remaining genes.

The default `removeBelow = 0.05` asks for genes that are detected in at least
5% of the pixels. With the large spots of other technologies, where every
spot contains several cells and many counts, this removes noise. A small bin
with few counts is different: a gene is only detected in the bins that
contain a cell expressing it, and often not even there. Marker genes of
cell-types that make up a small part of the tissue are therefore detected in
far fewer than 5% of the bins.

Here is the fraction of bins in which some well-known marker genes of kidney
cell-types are detected:

```{r markers}
markers <- c("proximal tubule S1" = "Slc5a2", "proximal tubule" = "Slc34a1",
             "proximal tubule S3" = "Slc7a13", "thick ascending limb" = "Umod",
             "distal convoluted tubule" = "Slc12a3", "principal cell" = "Aqp2",
             "intercalated cell" = "Atp6v1b1", "intercalated cell B" = "Slc26a4",
             "podocyte" = "Nphs2", "juxtaglomerular cell" = "Ren1",
             "endothelial cell" = "Emcn", "fibroblast" = "Col1a1",
             "smooth muscle" = "Acta2", "macrophage" = "C1qa",
             "urothelium" = "Upk1b")
detected <- rowSums(counts[markers, ] > 0) / ncol(counts)
data.frame(celltype = names(markers), gene = markers,
           percent.of.bins = round(100 * detected, 2), row.names = NULL)
```

More than half of these genes are detected in less than 5% of the bins.
With the default setting, the model would never see them:

```{r corpus_default}
corpusDefault <- restrictCorpus(counts, removeAbove = 1.0, removeBelow = 0.05,
                                verbose = FALSE)
dim(corpusDefault)
setdiff(markers, rownames(corpusDefault))
```

Only `r nrow(corpusDefault)` genes are left, and podocytes, juxtaglomerular
cells, intercalated cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle, macrophages and
urothelium have lost their marker genes. Podocytes, for example, are found
only in the glomeruli, which fill about half a percent of the bins.

With `removeBelow = 0.005` (half a percent of the bins, here about
`r format(round(0.005 * ncol(counts)), big.mark = ",")` bins) the full 1,000
genes are selected and all of these markers are among them:

```{r corpus}
corpus <- restrictCorpus(counts, removeAbove = 1.0, removeBelow = 0.005,
                         verbose = FALSE)
dim(corpus)
setdiff(markers, rownames(corpus))
```

As a rule of thumb, set `removeBelow` below the fraction of the pixels that
you expect the rarest cell-type of interest to occupy. A gene that is
detected in a few thousand bins is still supported by plenty of data, so
there is little risk in a low value for a dataset of this size.

`fitLDA()` needs a pixels x genes matrix in which each pixel has at least one
count:

```{r transpose}
corpus <- t(corpus)
corpus <- corpus[rowSums(corpus) > 0, ]
dim(corpus)
mean(rowSums(corpus))
```

# Fitting the models: `max.counts`

An LDA model has two parts: the gene expression profile of each cell-type
(`beta`, shared by all pixels) and the proportions of the cell-types in each
pixel (`theta`). Fitting alternates between the two, and nearly all the time
is spent on the proportions of the pixels, again and again while the
profiles improve.

The profiles are estimated from the counts of all pixels together. Beyond a
few million counts they hardly change when more pixels are added, so there
is no need to visit every pixel in every iteration. With `max.counts`,
`fitLDA()`

1. picks pixels at random until they have `max.counts` counts together,
2. fits the model on these pixels only,
3. computes the cell-type proportions of **all** pixels with the fitted
   profiles, which takes a single pass over the data.

The models that are returned contain the proportions of all pixels, and the
perplexity is computed on all pixels as well, so everything downstream works
as usual.

The limit is on the number of counts and not on the number of pixels because
the counts are what the profiles are estimated from: the fewer counts a
pixel has, the more pixels are needed. `max.counts = 5e6` (5 million counts)
is a good value for any bin size.

To see the effect, we fit a model with 12 cell-types on all bins and on a
subset. Set `ncores` to the number of cores of your computer; the bins are
processed in parallel.

```{r fit_compare}
ncores <- parallel::detectCores()

system.time(
  ldaAll <- fitLDA(corpus, Ks = 12, ncores = ncores, plot = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
)

system.time(
  ldaSubset <- fitLDA(corpus, Ks = 12, ncores = ncores, plot = FALSE, max.counts = 5e6)
)
```

The second fit used about a tenth of the bins and is several times faster.
The two models describe the data equally well. The perplexity (lower is
better) of both is computed on all bins:

```{r fit_compare_perplexity}
c(all = ldaAll$perplexities, subset = ldaSubset$perplexities)
```

Their cell-types are the same, too. We match the cell-types of the two models
and look at the correlation of their gene expression profiles:

```{r fit_compare_beta}
betaAll <- getBetaTheta(ldaAll$models[[1]], perc.filt = 0, verbose = FALSE)$beta
betaSubset <- getBetaTheta(ldaSubset$models[[1]], perc.filt = 0, verbose = FALSE)$beta
corMtx <- getCorrMtx(betaAll, betaSubset, type = "b", verbose = FALSE)
pairs <- lsatPairs(corMtx)
round(sort(corMtx[cbind(pairs$rowix, pairs$colsix)]), 2)
```

Nearly all cell-types of one model have a counterpart with almost the same
profile in the other. Do not expect a perfect match for every cell-type: LDA
models fitted from different starting points differ in this way as well,
typically by dividing one group of similar cells differently.

## Choosing the number of cell-types

The number of cell-types `K` is chosen by fitting models for a range of
values. With `max.counts` this takes seconds per model. `warm.start = TRUE`
saves more time: the model with the largest `K` is fitted first, and each
smaller model starts from the previous one after merging its two most
similar cell-types, instead of starting from scratch.

```{r fit, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
system.time(
  ldas <- fitLDA(corpus, Ks = seq(6, 24, by = 2), ncores = ncores,
                 max.counts = 5e6, warm.start = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
)
```

The perplexity (red) improves up to `K = 12` to `14` and gets worse after
that, while the number of cell-types with a mean proportion below 5% (blue)
grows with `K`. In a tissue that is
measured at this resolution, cell-types with a small mean proportion are
expected (see the glomeruli above), so we do not take them as a sign of
overfitting here, and continue with the model with the lowest perplexity.

```{r optimal}
optLDA <- optimalModel(models = ldas, opt = "min")
optLDA
```

# Results

```{r results}
results <- getBetaTheta(optLDA, perc.filt = 0.05, betaScale = 1000, verbose = FALSE)
deconProp <- results$theta
deconGexp <- results$beta
dim(deconProp)
```

The genes that are most specific to each cell-type, by their fold change
over the mean of all cell-types:

```{r top_genes}
foldChange <- log2(t(t(deconGexp + 1e-6) / (colMeans(deconGexp) + 1e-6)))
topSpecific <- t(apply(foldChange, 1, function(x) names(sort(x, decreasing = TRUE))[1:8]))
data.frame(mean.proportion = round(colMeans(deconProp), 3),
           top.genes = apply(topSpecific, 1, paste, collapse = " "))
```

`vizTopGenes()` shows the same genes as a dot plot. The largest dot of a
gene is at the cell-type with its highest expression:

```{r top_genes_plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=11, dpi=130}
vizTopGenes(results, n = 4)
```

Several cell-types are easy to recognise: the first segment of the proximal
tubule (cell-type 12: *Slc5a2*), the thick ascending limb (2: *Umod*,
*Cldn16*), the distal convoluted tubule (1: *Slc12a3*, *Calb1*), the
collecting duct (10: *Aqp6*, *Foxi1*, *Hsd11b2*) and the fat next to the
kidney (13: *Ucp1*, *Cidea*, *Fabp4*).

The cell-types in which the marker genes from above are most specific:

```{r marker_celltypes}
inCorpus <- markers[markers %in% colnames(foldChange)]
data.frame(celltype = names(inCorpus), gene = inCorpus,
           deconvolved.celltype = apply(foldChange[, inCorpus], 2, which.max),
           log2.fold.change = round(apply(foldChange[, inCorpus], 2, max), 1),
           row.names = NULL)
```

The marker genes that the default `removeBelow` would have removed are used
by the model: the intercalated cell markers are specific to the collecting
duct cell-type, and the others to cell-type 14, which combines smooth muscle
and urothelium (*Acta2*, *Myh11*, *Upk1b*, *Upk3a*) with other rare cells.
With `K = 14`, the rarest cells do not get a cell-type of their own; a model
with a larger `K` divides them further.

## Maps

With hundreds of thousands of bins, drawing a pie chart for every bin with
`vizAllTopics()` is neither fast nor readable. `vizTopicMaps()` draws one
map per cell-type. With more than 20000 pixels it draws an image instead of
a point for each pixel: here each cell of the image is the mean of 3 x 3
bins (see its argument `resolution`). With `scale = "free"`, each panel has
its own color scale, from 0 to the largest proportion of the cell-type,
which is stated in the title of the panel:

```{r maps, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, dpi=130}
vizTopicMaps(results, pos, scale = "free")
```

`vizDominantTopic()` summarises all cell-types in one map, with the
cell-type that has the highest proportion in each cell of the image:

```{r dominant, fig.width=8, fig.height=7, dpi=130}
vizDominantTopic(results, pos)
```

A cell-type can be checked against its most specific genes with
`vizTopicMarkers()`. The bins with a high proportion of the cell-type
should be the bins where its genes are expressed:

```{r celltype_markers, fig.width=8, fig.height=8, dpi=130}
vizTopicMarkers(results, pos, counts, topic = "2")
```

`vizReport(results, pos, counts, file = "report.pdf")` writes all of these
figures, and one figure like the last one for every cell-type, to a PDF
file. For this dataset that takes about 20 seconds.

The pie charts are useful for a small region. Here are 60 x 60 bins (480 µm
x 480 µm) of the cortex, at the right edge of the section:

```{r zoom, fig.width=7, fig.height=6, dpi=130, message=FALSE}
center <- c(x = 670, y = -418)
region <- rownames(deconProp)[abs(pos[rownames(deconProp), "x"] - center["x"]) < 30 &
                              abs(pos[rownames(deconProp), "y"] - center["y"]) < 30]
vizAllTopics(deconProp[region, ], pos[region, ], r = 0.5, lwd = 0) +
  guides(colour = "none")
```

# What about the 2 µm squares?

The 2 µm squares can be analysed in the same way, with two more changes.
They contain very few counts:

```{r load_2um}
cd2 <- read10xH5(paste0(f, files[3]))
dim(cd2)
summary(colSums(cd2))
```

- `min.lib.size = 100` in `cleanCounts()` would remove
  `r round(100 * mean(colSums(cd2) < 100))`% of the squares. Use a small value
  such as 10.
- `removeBelow` needs to be lower still, for example 0.001: the default of
  0.05 leaves `r sum(rowSums(cd2 > 0) > 0.05 * ncol(cd2))` genes.

`max.counts = 5e6` needs no change. This is where a limit on the counts
instead of the pixels matters: 5 million counts are about 50,000 of the 8 µm
bins, but about 700,000 of the 2 µm squares.

However, we recommend fitting the models on the 8 µm bins, as above. A
square with a handful of counts in the selected genes says very little
about which cell-types it contains. The model can still learn expression
profiles from millions of such squares, but in our tests the profiles were
less distinct than those of the 8 µm bins, the fit needed about 140
iterations instead of about 20, and every cell-type ended up with a similar
mean proportion.

If you want maps at the resolution of 2 µm, you can apply the model of the
8 µm bins to the 2 µm squares. `getBetaTheta()` computes the cell-type
proportions of new pixels when it is given their counts:

```{r transfer}
corpus2 <- t(cd2[colnames(corpus), ])
corpus2 <- corpus2[rowSums(corpus2) >= 3, ]
dim(corpus2)

system.time(
  deconProp2 <- getBetaTheta(optLDA, corpus = corpus2, perc.filt = 0,
                             ncores = ncores, verbose = FALSE)$theta
)
```

The names of the squares contain their row and column on the grid of 2 µm
squares; an 8 µm bin covers 4 x 4 of them. We look at the region from above
and at the cell-type that is most common in it, at both resolutions:

```{r transfer_map, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5, dpi=130}
rc <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(rownames(corpus2), "_|-"))
pos2 <- data.frame(x = (as.integer(rc[, 4]) + 0.5) / 4 - 0.5,
                   y = -((as.integer(rc[, 3]) + 0.5) / 4 - 0.5),
                   row.names = rownames(corpus2))
region2 <- rownames(pos2)[abs(pos2$x - center["x"]) < 30 & abs(pos2$y - center["y"]) < 30]
ct <- names(which.max(colMeans(deconProp[region, ])))

df <- rbind(data.frame(pos[region, ], proportion = deconProp[region, ct],
                       size = 1, bins = "8 µm bins"),
            data.frame(pos2[region2, ], proportion = deconProp2[region2, ct],
                       size = 0.25, bins = "2 µm squares, model of the 8 µm bins"))
df$bins <- factor(df$bins, levels = unique(df$bins))
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = proportion, width = size, height = size)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~ bins) +
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis(option = "A", direction = -1, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void() +
  ggtitle(paste("cell-type", ct))
```

The 2 µm map shows finer detail, but each square is noisy, and the squares
with fewer than 3 counts in the selected genes (white) were left out.

# Recommendations

| | large spots (ST, Visium) | Visium HD, 8 µm bins | Visium HD, 2 µm squares |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cleanCounts(min.lib.size = )` | 100 | 100 | 10 |
| `restrictCorpus(removeBelow = )` | 0.05 | 0.005 | 0.001 |
| `fitLDA(max.counts = )` | not needed | 5e6 | 5e6 |
| `fitLDA(warm.start = )` | optional | `TRUE` for a range of `Ks` | `TRUE` for a range of `Ks` |
| `fitLDA(ncores = )` | | all cores | all cores |

sessionInfo()
